implementation_notes: The application service is a @Service bean and its transaction boundary is the @Transactional annotation, applied by an AOP proxy around the method, so the method body is orchestration only and the container commits or rolls back on exit. Two consequences of proxying decide correctness: only calls entering through the proxy are intercepted, so self-invocation runs without any transaction, and rollback defaults to unchecked exceptions, so checked domain failures must be modelled as unchecked exceptions or listed in rollbackFor.
pitfalls: Self-invocation (this.otherMethod()) bypasses the proxy and silently runs without a transaction.
The default rollback rule covers unchecked exceptions only: a checked exception leaves the transaction committed.
Annotating a private, final or non-proxied method makes @Transactional a no-op; in proxy mode methods must be public (or protected since Spring 6).

variants.name: Stateless session bean with container-managed transactions (Jakarta EE)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic enterprise form of the same idea (the EJB example in Fowler's Service Layer): a @Stateless session bean implements the application operations and declares its transaction attributes, and the container's JTA transaction manager begins and commits around each method. Choose it when the runtime already is a Jakarta EE application server and distributed (XA) transactions or the container's declarative security model are required; Spring's proxies cover the same ground without an application server.
pitfalls: Container-managed transactions commit when the method returns, so work started after return (async listeners, callbacks) runs outside the transaction.
Calling a REQUIRES_NEW method on the same bean does not start a new transaction unless the bean invokes itself through an injected self-reference.
Stateless bean instances are pooled: per-request state kept in fields leaks between callers.
